source_text: ἀλλὰ τί ταῦτα θρηνῶ; ἔστιν ὁ σωτὴρ πάντων, καὶ τῶν ἡμιθανῶν καὶ τῶν λελῃστευμένων πάντων κηδεμὼν καὶ ἰατρός, λόγος ὁ ἄγρυπνος, φύλαξ πάντων ἀνθρώπων. ἔστιν ἡμῖν καὶ σπέρματα ἅ τε ἔχοντας ἡμᾶς ἀνέδειξας, καὶ ὅσα παρὰ σοῦ εἰλήφαμεν, τὰς καλὰς ὑποθήκας, σὺν οἷς ἄπιμεν. κλαίοντες μέν, ὡς πορευόμενοι, φέροντες δὲ σὺν αὐτοῖς ὅμως τὰ σπέρματα ταῦτα. ἴσως μὲν οὖν διασώσει ἡμᾶς ὁ φύλαξ ἐπιστάς· ἴσως δὲ ὑποστρέψομεν πρὸς σὲ πάλιν, φέροντες ἐκ τῶν σπερμάτων καὶ τοὺς καρποὺς καὶ τὰς δραγμίδας, τελείας μὲν οὐχί. πῶς γάρ; οἵας δὲ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν πολιτείᾳ πράξεων, διεφθαρμένας μὲν τῇ δυνάμει, ἢ ἀκάρπῳ ἢ κακοκάρπῳ τινί, μὴ καὶ προσδιαφθαρησομένῃ δὲ μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν, εἰ ὁ Θεὸς ἐπινεύοι.
thought_title: Comfort: the Savior keeps watch, and the seed goes with us
orientation: Gregory takes comfort: the Savior of all keeps watch, and the seeds Origen sowed go with him.
pass_a_gloss: But why do I lament these things? There is the Savior of all, both of the half dead and of all the robbed a guardian and physician, the sleepless Word, keeper of all men. There are for us also seeds, both those which you showed us having, and as many as from you we have received, the fine counsels, with which we depart. Weeping, as journeying, yet carrying with us nonetheless these seeds. Perhaps then the keeper, standing by, will preserve us through; perhaps we shall return to you again, bringing from the seeds both the fruits and the sheaves, not perfect indeed. For how? But such as possible for us from the actions in public life, spoiled by the power, some barren or bad-fruited one, yet not one about to be further spoiled with us, if God should assent.

pass_b_english: But why do I lament like this? There is the Savior of all, the guardian and physician of all who are half dead and all who have been robbed (Luke 10:30–34): the Word who never sleeps, the keeper of all people. We have seeds too: those you showed us we already had, and those we have received from you, your good counsels; with these we go. We go weeping, as people setting out on a journey, yet carrying these seeds with us all the same (Psalm 126:6). Perhaps, then, the Keeper will stand over us and bring us safely through; and perhaps we shall return to you again, bringing from the seeds both the fruits and the sheaves (Psalm 126:6). They will not be perfect; how could they be? They will be such as we are able to bring from the business of public life: spoiled, it is true, by some power that is barren or bears bad fruit, yet a power that, if God consents, will not be ruined further along with us.
notes: Psalm numbering: going out weeping with seed and returning with sheaves is LXX Psalm 125:6 (πορευόμενοι ἐπορεύοντο καὶ ἔκλαιον βάλλοντες τὰ σπέρματα ... αἴροντες τὰ δράγματα αὐτῶν), English Psalm 126:6; cited at both the weeping and the sheaves. 'The half dead and the robbed' continues the image of the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10:30-34), whose helper tends and heals him. Left uncited as uncertain: 'the Word who never sleeps, the keeper' may echo Psalm 121:4 (LXX 120:4, 'the one who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep'), but the wording differs (ἄγρυπνος, φύλαξ); 'the Savior of all' may echo 1 Timothy 4:10. 'Word' and 'Savior' are capitalized as Christ; 'the Keeper' is capitalized where it names him as a title. 'δραγμίδας' as printed (sheaves; the LXX has δράγματα). The first ἢ before ἀκάρπῳ has unusual breathing marks in the print and is read as ἢ ... ἢ. The last clause is compressed: the feminine datives (τῇ δυνάμει ... τινί ... προσδιαφθαρησομένῃ) agree, so it is 'the power', not the sheaves, that will not be ruined further; the English keeps that construction. The power may be the corrupting force of public business or Gregory's own capacity; the English leaves it open. The facing Latin of the Paris 1622 print takes the last clause the same way ('corruptos quidem facultate vel infrugifera, vel malae alicuius frugis; sed non amplius apud nos corrumpenda, si Deus annuerit').
